newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH STTK TARGETS LOW-PAY-RISE 2-YR INCOMES DEAL.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH STTK TARGETS LOW-PAY-RISE 2-YR INCOMES DEAL.

text.p: The Confederation of Salaried Employees (STTK), Finland's second biggest trade union group, said on Monday it aimed for a two-year incomes settlement from February 1998 with moderate nominal pay rises and spiced with income tax cuts.

STTK's council on Monday outlined targets for the next round of incomes settlement talks due in the autumn. The 600,000-member central union's board will define more precise pay deal targets at a meeting on May 12, STTK said in a statement.
The council said workers' purchasing power should rise.

Increased real earnings should be achieved through a combination of moderate pay rises and income tax cuts focused on medium-wage earners. STTK chairman Esa Swanljung said this meant employees earning 8,000-14,500 markka per month.

While looking for a centralised wage deal, STTK would not necessarily seek an agreement as tightly binding on the unions as the existing wage settlement because of the "different pressures" that existed in different sectors, Swanljung said.
Swanljung said it was "quite significant" that all unions had embraced the goal of lowering taxes, but finding a common tune among them for tax-cut demands would still not be easy.
"We have not yet discussed whether we will weld together our tax objectives, and I consider it entirely possible that this would not be easy to achieve," Swanljung said.

The link between the unions' support for Finnish membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU) and the incomes settlement was apparent, even if the unions had not yet articulated it, Swanljung said.
"I have not seen a desire to link (EMU and the incomes package), but in practice they have quite a big mutual link," Swanljung said.

Asked whether the unions would go so far as to block EMU membership if buffer funds were not created to cushion potential asymetric shocks to the economy, Swanlung said: "That would be too drastic a conclusion."
A joint communique on EMU by trade unions and employers' organisations could be ready for publication in early June, Swanljung said and played down the difficulties involved.
"Discussions have been conducted in a good spirit and I consider it realistic ... that it could be ready at the beginning of June," he said.
The STTK's objectives would include demands for changes in working life such as a demand for shorter working hours, the STTK council said in the statement.
"The shortening of working hours must, in the view of the STTK council, substantially improve employment," it said.
Asked how realistic a two-year agreement was, Swanljung said: "I think it is possible, and conditions for it exist."
